notes: Parole recall JR; Burnton J on charge-only risk assessment and oral hearing fairness is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Broadbent v Parole Board: recall on pending drug charge
key_facts: Mr Broadbent was released on parole in October 2003 after serving half of a 12-year sentence for armed robbery.
In January 2004 he was arrested driving a van containing about 40 kilograms of cannabis and charged with possession with intent to supply and later conspiracy.
The Home Secretary recalled him to prison on his probation officer's recommendation; the Parole Board rejected his representations without an oral hearing.
He remained in custody despite conditional bail because of licence revocation, and sought judicial review of the Board's January and February 2005 decisions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Parole Board decisions refusing release on licence following recall for alleged breach of a good-behaviour licence condition.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no relief granted because an imminent fresh Parole Board hearing and criminal trial made quashing earlier decisions pointless, though the court gave guidance on lawful decision-making.
enrichment.ratio: A pending charge and prosecution alone cannot rationally establish a risk of reoffending for parole purposes without more, but undisputed facts such as driving a van containing a large hidden cannabis consignment may suffice; the Board must consider oral hearing requests and may defer until after trial where investigation would be unfair.
legal_issues: Whether a charge and pending prosecution alone can justify refusing parole release
Relevance of Crown Court bail and prosecution's non-reliance on reoffending risk
Whether the Parole Board had to grant an oral hearing under Smith and West principles
Appropriate relief where a fresh Parole Board hearing was imminent
index_terms: R (Smith and West) v Parole Board
linked_authorities: R (Smith and West) v The Parole Board [2005] UKHL 1
R (Brooks) v The Parole Board [2004] EWCA Civ 80

notes: Novel clinical case manager issues on interim payment; Court of Appeal rejects joint instruction and expert-equivalent witness direction.

enrichment.short_title: Wright v Sullivan: clinical case manager and interim damages
key_facts: A young woman suffered severe brain injury in a road accident; liability was compromised 70/30 against the defendant driver.
Her receiver sought a £50,000 interim payment under CPR 25.7 to appoint a clinical case manager and fund immediate care.
The defendant's insurers wanted the case manager jointly instructed, full disclosure of communications, and no closed-door access by the claimant's team.
Wakerley J granted the interim payment without conditions but directed that the case manager's witness statement should follow expert-report duties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from an interim payment order in a high-value personal injury damages assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Defendant's appeal dismissed with costs; claimant's cross-appeal allowed with costs and the judge's expert-equivalent direction deleted.
enrichment.ratio: A clinical case manager in litigation owes therapeutic duties to the patient alone, not to the defendant's insurers; joint instruction and compelled waiver of litigation privilege are impermissible, and a case manager giving evidence is a witness of fact not subject to CPR Part 35.
legal_issues: Whether interim payment could be conditioned on joint instruction of a clinical case manager
Whether defendants could require disclosure of privileged communications with the case manager
Whether a case manager's witness statement should recite expert duties to the court
Interaction between Rehabilitation Code collaboration and therapeutic confidentiality
linked_authorities: Waugh v British Railways Board [1980] AC 521

confidence.notes: Novel procedural issues and both appellate dispositions are explicitly reasoned.

notes: Late quantum amendment in stale solicitor negligence claim; partial appeal allowed on capital appreciation distinction.

enrichment.short_title: McLouglin v Jones: late schedule of loss in negligence claim
key_facts: The claimant was wrongly convicted in 1993 of robbery and GBH after allegedly deficient defence work by the defendant solicitors.
He issued a writ in 1998 claiming loss of liberty, earnings and rental income; the original schedule totalled about £556,000.
After years of delay he served a revised schedule in April 2005 claiming over £4 million, including loss of capital appreciation on sold and notional purchased properties.
Eady J struck out the new capital-appreciation and property-expansion claims shortly before a July 2005 trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against an interlocutory order striking out parts of an updated schedule of loss.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; appeal allowed in part to reinstate capital appreciation on properties sold because of the solicitors' breach, but claims based on acquisition of additional properties remained struck out.
enrichment.ratio: A revised schedule served under an order to update figures may not introduce wholly new heads of loss without permission; where a stale case is fixed for imminent trial, striking out oppressive late capital-appreciation claims based on hypothetical property purchases is justified, but loss on actually sold properties may remain part of the existing rental-income case.
legal_issues: Whether the revised schedule was an update or an impermissible amendment
Prejudice to defendants from new £4 million capital-appreciation claims before trial
Distinction between schedule 4 sold-property losses and schedule 5 hypothetical purchases
Exercise of discretion where both parties had contributed to delay

confidence.notes: Discretionary analysis and partial appellate reinstatement are clearly explained.

notes: Schedule 22 mandatory life tariff reviews; Lord Chief Justice reduced 12-year tariffs to 10 years for three joint-enterprise murderers.

enrichment.short_title: Middleton tariff review: Hanley street murder minimum terms
key_facts: Three men were convicted of murder after a violent disorder in Hanley in December 1996 in which Delroy Nedrick died from a fatal punch and subsequent kicks.
The trial judge recommended minimum terms of 10 to 12 years; Lord Bingham thought 10 years probably enough, but the Home Secretary set 12 years.
The applicants applied under Schedule 22 for review of the notified minimum terms after serving many years in prison with strong mitigation and rehabilitation progress.
The deaths arose from group violence in a public place; Coulson delivered the blow that caused Nedrick to fall and strike his head.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Related applications under paragraph 3 of Schedule 22 to the Criminal Justice Act 2003 for review of mandatory life minimum terms.
enrichment.outcome: Minimum term for each applicant reduced from 12 years to 10 years, less respective time spent on remand.
enrichment.ratio: On Schedule 22 review the court may take account of post-sentence progress and remorse; where there was no intention to kill, group violence without weapons, provocation and exceptional prison rehabilitation, a 12-year tariff was not required for retribution and deterrence when the Lord Chief Justice had recommended 10 years.
legal_issues: Application of Schedule 21 starting points by analogy without retroactivity breach
Whether racist aggravation under paragraph 5(2)(g) applied
Relevance of exceptional prison progress under Cole principles
Differentiation between Middleton, Coulson and Bauer
linked_authorities: R (Cole & Others) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWHC 1789 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Individual tariff decisions and reasons for departing from the Secretary of State are fully set out.

notes: Leading Court of Appeal decision rejecting medical necessity defence for personal cannabis use.

enrichment.short_title: Quayle v R: medical necessity and cannabis offences
key_facts: Five defendants appealed convictions for cultivating, possessing or importing cannabis for personal use to relieve severe chronic pain.
Medical experts accepted cannabis gave some of the appellants meaningful pain and sleep relief where conventional medication had failed or caused unacceptable side effects.
Some trial judges had left necessity to the jury; others had ruled the defence unavailable as a matter of law.
The Attorney General also referred a case in which a jury had acquitted on a medical necessity direction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Five appeals against conviction and one Attorney General's reference on the availability of medical necessity for cannabis offences.
enrichment.outcome: All appeals dismissed; the Attorney General's reference answered in the negative; medical necessity is not available for these cannabis offences.
enrichment.ratio: English law does not recognise a defence of medical necessity or duress of circumstances permitting otherwise unlawful personal cultivation, possession or importation of cannabis to alleviate pain; allowing severe pain to equate to serious injury would create an undesirable policy-based licence dependent on personal vulnerability.
legal_issues: Availability of necessity or duress of circumstances for cannabis use to relieve pain
Whether severe pain may be equated with serious injury or threat to life
Relevance of Canadian R v Parker and medical treatment cases such as Gillick and Re F
Whether continuous self-help cannabis use could ever satisfy necessity
linked_authorities: Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech Area Health Authority [1986] 1 AC 142
In re F (Mental Patient: Sterilisation) [1990] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Comprehensive appellate treatment and explicit negative answer to the reference.

notes: Long GMC performance hearing quashed; Collins J found insufficient evidence of seriously deficient team-working alone.

enrichment.short_title: Wilson v GMC: seriously deficient performance appeal
key_facts: Dr Wilson, a consultant anaesthetist at an RAF hospital in Cyprus, faced GMC performance proceedings after complaints about team-working, record-keeping and conduct in 1998-1999.
An assessment panel found seriously deficient performance; after failed statement-of-requirements retraining the case went to a CPP hearing lasting 41 days.
The CPP found seriously deficient performance based mainly on unacceptable relationships with colleagues, imposing 15 months of conditional registration.
The doctor appeared in person for much of the hearing and argued the complaints arose from a dysfunctional military department and exaggerated allegations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 40 against a Committee on Professional Performance finding of seriously deficient performance and conditional registration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; CPP decision quashed; conditional registration direction set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Section 36A performance proceedings examine past professional performance on the balance of probabilities and require particulars and fair disclosure akin to conduct cases; isolated team-working difficulties in an exceptionally dysfunctional workplace, without substantiated patient risk, may be insufficient for a finding of seriously deficient performance warranting mandatory conditions.
legal_issues: Construction of section 36A and the distinction between performance and misconduct
Effect of Krippendorf and Sadler on assessment of seriously deficient performance
Fairness of CPP procedure, disclosure and use of hearsay
Whether team-working failures alone in a military hospital justified serious deficiency
linked_authorities: Krippendorf v General Medical Council [2001] Lloyds Rep Med 8
Sadler v General Medical Council [2003] UKPC 59

notes: Section 58 MHA compulsory medication upheld; Collins J rejected opposing psychiatrist's evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Taylor v Haydn-Smith: compulsory antipsychotic treatment
key_facts: Roger Taylor was detained under section 37 with a section 41 restriction order after convictions for affray and common assault linked to persistent delusional disorder.
He was conditionally discharged in November 2003 but recalled in October 2004 after stopping medication and deteriorating.
Doctors certified under section 58(3)(b) that antipsychotic medication should be given without consent; he challenged this by judicial review with expert evidence from Dr Azuonye.
His history included manslaughter, rape, persecutionary delusions about professionals and prior benefit from medication before discharge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review, with an initial interim injunction, of certificates authorising non-consensual antipsychotic treatment under section 58.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; compulsory antipsychotic treatment under section 58 was lawful; injunction discharged.
enrichment.ratio: On judicial review the court must reach its own conclusion on medical necessity where Convention rights are engaged; persistent delusional disorder requiring antipsychotic treatment may be established despite a patient's denial of illness, especially where prior medication had alleviated his condition and recall followed non-compliance.
legal_issues: Whether medical necessity for treatment was convincingly shown under Herczegfalvy principles
Whether the court should hear oral evidence from treating doctors and SOAD
Capacity to consent under section 58 and irrational refusal of treatment
Weight to be given to a Mental Health Review Tribunal finding later quashed
linked_authorities: Wilkinson v Broadmoor Special Hospital [2002] 1 WLR 419

confidence.notes: Medical necessity and rejection of opposing expert evidence are clearly reasoned.

notes: Property development profit-share trial; Evans-Lombe J rejected partnership and trust claims but left quantum inquiry on work done.

enrichment.short_title: Patel v Euro Investments: failed 25% development profit claim
key_facts: Raj Patel claimed a 25% share in profits from developing a former British Rail club property in Kentish Town bought by Euro Investments for about £1 million.
He alleged a joint enterprise or understanding at a 'Third Meeting' with Mr Gami and Mr Pinduria giving him one quarter of the development profits.
He had assisted with acquisition, planning, valuations and site management, and lent substantial sums to Mr Gami.
The defendants denied any Third Meeting or profit-sharing agreement and said Raj acted as an unpaid helper or lender only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claim for a 25% interest in the property or company shares and related monetary remedies.
enrichment.outcome: Claim for a quarter interest in the property or Euro failed on all equitable and restitutionary grounds; admitted debt claims for loans survived and quantum for work done was left for inquiry unless agreed.
enrichment.ratio: A claimant seeking a share in development profits must prove a consensual arrangement or understanding; where the alleged Third Meeting is rejected on the facts, neither partnership, resulting or constructive trust nor unjust enrichment can succeed simply because the claimant contributed unpaid work based on a mistaken belief in entitlement.
legal_issues: Whether a partnership or joint enterprise existed without a concluded contract
Whether a resulting or constructive trust arose from the alleged Third Meeting
Availability of unjust enrichment by analogy with proprietary estoppel
Quantum of debt and payment for work on the property
linked_authorities: Banque Financière de la Cité v Parc (Battersea) Ltd [1999] 1 AC 221
Banner Homes Group plc v Luff Developments Ltd [2000] Ch 372

notes: Traveller eviction JR failed on site provision and welfare enquiry challenges; bound by Price v Leeds.

enrichment.short_title: Kanssen v DEFRA: Traveller eviction from Rendlesham Forest
key_facts: Mr Kanssen, a Traveller, camped on Forestry Commission land at Rendlesham Forest with Alice Futter and three children from Easter 2004.
A county court possession order over the forest had been obtained in March 2004; the Commission sought to enforce it by warrant of restitution.
The Commission wrote to local authorities requesting welfare enquiries under government guidance but received no substantive response before proceeding.
The claimant argued the Commission had power to provide transit sites and had failed to make adequate welfare enquiries before eviction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Forestry Commission's decision to enforce a possession order against unauthorised Traveller encampment.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; enforcement decision held lawful on both site-provision and welfare-enquiry grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Forestry legislation does not empower the Forestry Commission to provide residential Traveller sites; as a public body without welfare expertise it may reasonably rely on written requests to local authorities and need not conduct its own enquiries before eviction where Article 8 cannot be raised as a defence to possession under Price v Leeds.
legal_issues: Whether the Forestry Commission had power to provide Traveller transit sites
Extent of welfare enquiries required before enforcing possession
Application of ODPM Guidance on Managing Unauthorised Camping February 2004
Effect of Price v Leeds on Article 8 defences to possession
linked_authorities: Price & Others v Leeds City Council [2005] EWCA Civ 389
R v Lincolnshire County Council ex parte Atkinson (1996) 8 Admin LR 529

confidence.notes: Both limbs of the challenge and reliance on Price are clearly resolved.

notes: Article 2 inquest scope JR; Wilson J quashed coroner's broad child protection inquest ruling.

enrichment.short_title: Plymouth v Coroner: Article 2 scope of Perrin inquest
key_facts: Nine-month-old Perrin died from bronchopneumonia aggravated by dehydration in July 2002 while under intensive social services monitoring.
His mother and her partner later pleaded guilty to cruelty by failing to seek medical attention that would probably have saved him.
The coroner ruled the inquest should investigate whether Plymouth and other agencies contributed to his death through systemic child protection failures.
Plymouth sought judicial review to limit the inquest to the final two days of Perrin's life rather than his whole life and agency conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a coroner's preliminary ruling on the scope of a jury inquest into a child's death.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; coroner's ruling that Article 2 required a broadened inquest into agency failings was quashed; declaration that the investigative duty was not engaged on the available evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Article 2's operational duty is triggered only where authorities knew or ought to have known of a real and immediate risk to life; intensive prior support without such knowledge at the relevant time does not require a coroner to investigate systemic child protection failures across the child's life.
legal_issues: When Article 2 investigative duty is engaged in child death inquests
Whether arguable breach existed where agencies provided exceptional support until the final days
Proper scope of an inquest into agency contribution to death
Whether the coroner erred in applying Osman principles to the facts
linked_authorities: Middleton v West Sussex Coroner [2004] EWCA Civ 861
